title: Energy: SA premier says the tech giants' demands 'crazy'
full_text:
South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas says the world's biggest technology companies have unrealistic expectations about the energy available to power their artificial intelligence aspirations in Australia, warning there is nowhere near enough renewable generation.
Malinauskas, who travelled to the United States in July to meet with AI developers and data centre operators, along with Democrats and Republicans, said demand for power was "just crazy stuff".
"One in particular I met with in the US said, 'You know, we're looking for a gigawatt in 2027'," he told The Australian Financial Review Infrastructure Summit. "Even if you had all the money in the world, and I accept some of these companies might, even if you applied all the money in the world at that and threw it at that problem, you could not procure that much new generation in that period of time, regardless of the source."
A boom in data centre construction, which has been underpinned by an explosion in AI processing, has become increasingly fraught as community anger and worries about power consumption have turned into political issues. In the US, a Democratic Party sweep in the midterms has created significant worries in the industry that projects will be delayed.
In Australia, Energy Minister Chris Bowen has asked the electricity network rulemaker to put in place rules that would force data centres to source round-the-clock power from entirely new renewable sources located in the same state, in the hope of preventing a drain on existing generation.
Data centres and their customers can currently buy power purchase certificates to offset grid use from renewable operators around the country.
Malinauskas, speaking in Sydney on Monday, said he was "pragmatic" about the use of gas generation for data centres, adding that he believed the fossil fuel had an essential role in supporting renewable energy sources.
"If you accept that new generation is critical to this endeavour, and it clearly must be ... then you need to factor in the time that it takes to actually get this new generation online, and I think that's the ultimate challenge," he said.
Some 30 data centres developments are being considered by South Australia, including two huge projects pitched by Australian developer Firmus in regional parts of the state, and another by Nasdaq-listed Iren.
The state's electricity transmission network owner, ElectraNet, is planning a 500-kilometre upgrade of high-voltage lines and substations to carry power to proposed data centres, but this is expected to take at least four years.
Speaking at the summit, Damian Secen, who oversees infrastructure at HMC Capital, said data centre companies should spend more time considering whether they could build AI-focused assets on the site of old power plants.
"I'm a huge fan [of converting sites]," said Secen, whose firm is a major investor in ASX-listed developer DigiCo Infrastructure REIT. "If you build in those centres, you'll attract a lot of industry, and you'll already have the social licence because you're in centres of existing employment."
Arash Shojaie, a partner at QIC Global Infrastructure, said he believed it was better to own the power and network than data centres themselves.
"No matter where you build the data centre, the power will always be needed. It's not sexy; you won't read it in the headlines, but it does provide a very similar exposure," said Shojaie, who sits on several energy boards.
The growing backlash has not only been limited to power consumption, but to worries about how data centres will dominate suburban areas. The pushback has led developers, including Goodman Group and AirTrunk, to pull projects, while NextDC has warned of delays at a major Melbourne asset.
That delay pushed shares in the ASX-listed NextDC down more than 42 per cent in 40 minutes after local uproar forced poles and wire operator Jemena to delay new power infrastructure needed for the expansion.
The Albanese government is exploring a ban on data centres being built near homes and recreational facilities, and Malinauskas said he supported the move, although he was against a moratorium on all projects.
"There are some really good examples in regional South Australia where I think [data centres] will be welcomed," he said, acknowledging public distrust in some developments because of a lack of transparency.
Nine Entertainment Co.
